crumbs.name: AI Adoption and Governance in Life Sciences

reading.body:
Three large drugmakers have signed company wide agreements with frontier AI labs instead of buying narrow tools. Sanofi went with OpenAI and Formation Bio in 2024, Novo Nordisk with OpenAI in April 2026, and Bristol Myers Squibb with Anthropic to put Claude across the business.

The pattern is consolidation at the top of the buyer. Each deal names one primary lab and describes use across discovery, trials, or the whole company, not a single workflow. That shifts the integration burden onto the vendor and gives the lab a durable enterprise account, which is the same dynamic that makes compute demand lumpy: a few very large customers committing at once rather than many small ones.

For AI specifically, the constraint these deals test is not model quality but whether a regulated company can run one vendor's systems through security review, validation, and production planning. The stated risk is dependence, and the stated mitigation is keeping critical workflows portable. The data does not say what any of these agreements cost, how they are structured, whether they are exclusive, or what results they have produced. It covers three announcements and no outcomes.

siblings.name: Governing AI in a Regulated Company

explainer:
Frontier AI labs build the most capable general models. Drugmakers sign strategic agreements with them for broad access across the company, early access to new capabilities, joint development of tools for research or operations, and support with deployment. Several of the largest pharma companies now have such agreements, often with one lab as a primary partner.

A single primary partner simplifies procurement, security review and training. The trade off is dependence on one vendor's roadmap, pricing and policies. Many companies therefore keep critical workflows portable, use model neutral integration layers, and evaluate other models for specific tasks.
